question: A digital health startup is about to launch a telemedicine platform on Google Cloud that will store protected health information (PHI) for patients in the United States. The compliance officer says that no PHI may be uploaded until the company's HIPAA obligations with Google are formally in place. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do first?
options: Open a support case asking Google to certify the telemedicine application as HIPAA compliant before go-live.
Enable Assured Workloads with the FedRAMP High control package, because it is a superset of HIPAA.
Review and accept the Google Cloud Business Associate Agreement (BAA) in the Cloud Console as an account administrator, and restrict the workload to services covered by the BAA.
Sign a separate BAA for each project by emailing the Google Cloud legal team a signed copy of your internal BAA template.
explanation: Under HIPAA, Google acts as a business associate, and the BAA must be in place before PHI is processed; Google offers a standard BAA that an account administrator accepts directly in the Cloud Console, and it covers the whole account rather than individual projects. After accepting it, you must restrict the workload to the services listed as covered under the BAA. Option A is wrong because Google does not certify customer applications; HIPAA has no certification body and compliance is a shared responsibility. Option B is wrong because FedRAMP is a US federal government framework, not a substitute for a BAA. Option D is wrong because Google uses its own standard BAA at the account level, not per-project custom agreements sent by email.
hint: Core Rule (HIPAA and BAA): Under HIPAA, Google acts as a business associate, and the BAA must be in place before PHI is processed; Google offers a standard BAA that an account administrator accepts directly in the Cloud Console, and it covers the whole account rather than individual projects.

question: A European e-commerce company stores order history in BigQuery and keeps seven years of immutable transaction archives in Cloud Storage buckets that have a retention policy locked for legal reasons. Under GDPR, customers exercise the right to erasure several times a day, and the data protection officer insists that erased customers' personal data must become unrecoverable even in the locked archives. You need a design that satisfies both the legal retention and the erasure requirement. What should you do?
options: Ask Google Cloud support to remove the retention lock on the affected objects so that individual archive files can be deleted on request.
Copy the archives into a new bucket without a retention policy, delete the affected records, and delete the original bucket.
Store the archives with a shorter retention period and rely on object lifecycle rules to delete personal data after 30 days.
Encrypt each customer's personal data with a per-customer data encryption key before archiving, keep the keys in a separate store, and destroy the customer's key when an erasure request is received.
explanation: Crypto-shredding is the recognized pattern for reconciling immutable retention with erasure: personal fields are encrypted with a per-data-subject key (wrapped by Cloud KMS), and destroying that key renders the archived data permanently unreadable without modifying the locked objects. Option A is wrong because a locked retention policy cannot be removed by anyone, including Google, which is precisely what makes it defensible for legal hold. Option B defeats the purpose of the legal retention control and would breach the retention obligation. Option C ignores the seven-year legal retention requirement. This solution reflects the security, privacy and compliance pillar of the Well-Architected Framework by separating key management from data storage.
hint: Core Rule (GDPR right to erasure): Crypto-shredding is the recognized pattern for reconciling immutable retention with erasure: personal fields are encrypted with a per-data-subject key (wrapped by Cloud KMS), and destroying that key renders the archived data permanently unreadable without modifying the locked objects.
